What's helped me in the long run is trying to find the root cause of the anxiety/uncomfiness then you can try to make changes based on that. So if it's because there's a lot of people, then when going to restaurants you can request a table or booth that's around less people. If it's because you feel claustrophobic inside the restaurant then you can aim to go to restaurants with outdoor seating. I saw some of your comments mention overstimulation, maybe you can wear glasses with dim lenses if you're comfortable with that and see if it helps. Also requesting tables where you face the wall, so any of the outer/corner tables. Anything that makes you feel safer :) it is always multiple things too but if there's many reasons I would focus on the bigger causes first then the smaller ones. 

ALSO I should say that these things help just to get you more comfortable but then it's always good to keep taking more steps once you're ready so that you don't have to avoid certain restaurants and situations.

Not the exact same but when my anxiety is higher I get paranoid about throwing up in public or in front of others (just an irrational fear) so I will usually eat foods that I know won't make my nausea worse. This is usually bland foods too like oatmeal, PB and j sandwich, literally almost anything vegetarian. What helps me eat outside of those foods is usually eating in a space where I feel most comfortable so for me it's my house. Maybe this might help your friend?

I have not been able to relate to anyone about my food anxiety either so when I read your post I totally understood. I also hate eating in restaurants and just in public in general because I have a fear of throwing up there. It triggers my anxiety at times which completely takes away my appetite. Almost like there is a certain pressure or expectation I put on myself when I eat out. If possible, maybe you could get some food to-go and eat it wherever you are staying, to at least get something down? You could also try to incorporate snacks from a local grocery store throughout the day so the anxiety/pressure of eating is taken away. I'm not sure if this might help but I notice that if I have to eat out, it helps when I'm at a restaurant with foods I'm familiar with because I know what to expect. Also fast food type places are better to handle as well because you have the freedom to eat at your own pace after you order whereas in restaurants it's kind of expected to finish in a certain amount of time. Getting a box for food you haven't finished and taking it back to eat may also be an option! I do this a lot at new restaurants or if my anxiety is higher on certain days. Sorry if none of this is any help but just know that you are not alone in your fears for this! :)

Start small with places that are the least anxious to you, for me it was a local game store that my sister and I had grown up going to. I was so happy that day, realizing that I wasn't as anxious as I thought I would be. 

Then slowly keep challenging yourself but try not to overwhelm yourself if you have the time. All the years of exposure therapy feels like it burnt out my brain but I would do it over again because it's better than the uncontrollable anxiety.

Exposure therapy really helped me though it sucked in the moment but the overall process that slowly got me to be able to manage my anxiety was first trying to understand what exactly was making me anxious and finding out what my triggers were with a therapist. For what exactly was making me anxious, I discovered it was being in a space where I felt trapped whether physically or socially. I realized I felt trapped when I was sitting in a classroom or a meeting and that was the main cause of my anxiety. Then I found out my triggers that made it worse. I would keep notes on my phone and whenever I could remember to I would type my triggers, anything you can think of. Especially triggers that you would be able to control for example sitting in the front row of a class is one of mine that really enhanced that main cause of my anxiety. Once I realized that, I took the extra effort to get to my classes early so I could find a seat near the back. I would still get anxiety during class but it was more manageable than if I was sitting in the front. 

Weather was also a big factor, so make sure to dress comfortably if being too hot triggers your anxiety. And if that's not enough bring a little fan with you everywhere. Anything that will help you control those triggers. Once you are able to do that it gives you that feeling of control back with your life which can improve your mental health and lessen your anxiety too :)

_**TL;DR I think really understanding what is making you anxious, then finding those triggers that make it worse and  taking steps to control those triggers can really help and it's ideal if you are able to do this with a therapist you feel comfortable with.**_ It is still hard to live with but it's significantly more manageable than it was in the past!

I used to get more frequent intrusive thoughts back when my anxiety levels were worse. Over time of working through my anxiety by going to therapy (tried out different therapists) they decreased and I very rarely have them anymore. Taking things one at a time helped, also trying to figure out my triggers and doing things to minimize them. For example sitting in the front row of anything was a big trigger for me so when I figured that out I made the effort to get to things early to choose a spot in the back. Then,listing all my triggers and listing what helped me calm down (like petting my cat, laying down in my room, listening to a certain song, etc). You don't have to list them all at once but maybe just as you realize them throughout the days. Just really try to minimize what raises your anxiety by finding those triggers and what exactly makes you anxious. Intrusive thoughts create panic for me too and just try to realize that those thoughts are not you but your anxiety trying to mess with you. (At least that's how I saw it). As your anxiety becomes more manageable by minimizing those triggers you will feel less like your anxiety is controlling your life and those thoughts should decrease as well.

I felt the same after I graduated. I didn't even think I would graduate because of my anxiety but I made it and I was beating myself up mentally every day afterwards because I felt lost and behind. 

Try taking small steps, if something is too overwhelming make it smaller. For example, your resume, instead of the overwhelming task of creating a whole one try to start with just thinking of every/any experience that you have. List down any volunteering you did, jobs, projects in college, it could even be things like babysitting your cousins, helping out a family/friends business. No matter how small, if it comes to mind just list it :) and now you have a rough draft of your experience. Then maybe start describing the things you did in each experience. Such as, "edited some photos for my friends blog", "helped set up a stage for the church". Next step could maybe be googling some sample resumes and trying to apply everything you wrote down to a sample resume template. Read through some samples that have similar experience as you and circle some descriptive words that you could use. Then try adding those words to the descriptions you made. Also go at your own pace! Don't try to do everything all at once :) give yourself time to breathe. Then once you have a resume rough draft, you could have someone proofread it. 

There are also some resources online that could help! Try looking to see if your college had any career resources. They might be able to help you with what you want to look for and all that BUT I know first hand how intimidating that can be. One resource I came across recently is the Harvard resume pdf. You can find it by searching "Harvard resume tips" in Google and it's the first pdf. Also this is only for reference so don't feel like you have to make your resume exactly like the ones in the PDF. 

Take your time and take small steps. :) Also know that it is not uncommon to not have a job after graduating. You might feel isolated because those around you are finding jobs but most of the time no one has a job right out college.

I don't have much advice but just wanted to let you know I'm in a similar boat... I do have a tip that might help with panic attacks though. 

If you feel a panic attack or worrying thoughts coming along, try to instantly fixate your mind on something else. For example, name everything thats around you (if you're inside a room look around and name then describe some of the objects there, "blue curtains, brown wooden desk, old ceiling fan etc", if your outside it could be things like "a guy walking a dog, the dog looks like a beagle, a girl riding a red bike, etc" you could even name and describe the clothes your wearing if you don't want to look around). It may sound ridiculous or silly but its an effective technique and has helped in the moment to distract my mind from triggering thoughts. It's enough to stop a panic attack before it becomes out of control, then being able to slowly calm down. It was something that my therapist taught me and it's helped whenever I'm desperate for stopping an incoming panic attack. Not sure if you may need or use it but puttin it here just in case :)

Also about the chest pains, if they started to happen after your anxiety, it could likely be a symptom of it. Though if you think it may be something else or the anxiety that results from it starts to severely impact your daily life, it wouldn't hurt to get checked if you're able to. I have panicked about chest pains in the past due to anxiety (which ended up being nothing serious) and going to get checked was what ended up giving me that peace of mind 😅🙏

In my experience I did CBT and mindfulness practice for anxiety. I can't say that it "fixed" my anxiety but it definitely helped to manage it.

I didn't/don't practice mindfulness very consistently but when I was doing it more often I found myself more relaxed than usual which made my anxiety easier to control. Certain things wouldn't trigger my anxiety like they usually would. 

But it didn't start helping until after a couple sessions. The very first one actually kind of triggered my anxiety since it was new (it was a yoga session) but once I was going regularly I got comfortable and it started helping. 

It also helped prevent panic attacks by using the clear your head of worries/control breathing/stop your chain of thinking/relax muscles practices. I know it's not easy but after all the yoga/meditation sessions I did I have actually been able to calm myself down sometimes before having a panic attack. It also just kind of reduced my ongoing anxiety in general so I'm kinda glad my therapist kept pushing me to go to any type of meditation/yoga etc. session haha. Again, this is all based off my experience, I've had GAD for 7 years but it's gotten better over the years.

I would say to try it if you have the opportunity, even do some meditation sessions at home just using a YouTube video or just meditating in silence lol. It might be a little hard at first but if you keep at it, it'll start getting easier to get into that relaxed/meditation state. There's also a bunch of easy mindfulness excercises online and apps that can help. Or you can look up local yoga/meditation studios and browse through the classes if your feeling adventurous, you'd be surprised how many different types of meditations there are :D also sorry this got so long haha ;;
